clue.text: Plant housed in another building

indicators.note: something housed is kept inside a home, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A potted plant kept in a different building, like a greenhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the two words: anot-HER B-uilding.
explanation.definitionFit: Basil, mint and parsley are all examples of this small leafy kind of plant used in cooking.

clue.text: Firm beginning to build key metallic element

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word
the Alt key on a computer keyboard

explanation.surface: A company starting to build a key out of some metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' is not a lock key or a musical key but the Alt key on a keyboard.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobalt is a chemical element, a hard bluish-grey metal with atomic number 27.

clue.text: Near enough to be involved in one of two charitable actions?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: approximately, allowing a small margin
second meaning, read literally: a choice between two acts of handing over or receiving

explanation.walkthrough: Read word by word, the phrase offers a choice between two actions, one of them the generous act of giving; the question mark admits that taking is hardly charitable.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means roughly or approximately, as in 'ten minutes, more or less', allowing a small error either way.

clue.text: Tribe's unusual colour

indicators.note: something unusual is out of its normal form, so these letters take a different order

parts.note: the possessive 's supplies the final S

explanation.surface: A tribe with a distinctive or strange colour of its own.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is ignored, as is usual in crosswords, so the possessive gives a plain plural to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Bistre is a brownish pigment made from soot, used by artists for wash drawings, so it names a particular shade.

clue.text: Compliantly offering a word of prayer — competently, too

parts.note: the word said at the close of a prayer
doing something competently is doing it skilfully

explanation.surface: Someone obediently saying a prayer, and doing it well too.
explanation.walkthrough: The two adverb-like halves join directly: AMEN then ABLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Being amenable means willingly agreeing or yielding, so acting this way is behaving in a cooperative, obedient manner.

clue.text: A revolutionary can be a pain

parts.note: taken as written
Che Guevara, the Argentine Marxist revolutionary

explanation.surface: A rebel can be a real nuisance to those in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A pain' sounds like slang for a nuisance, but it is meant literally as physical hurt; Che is the crossword's go-to revolutionary.
explanation.definitionFit: An ache is a continuous dull bodily hurt, so it is a synonym for a pain felt in the body.

clue.text: Living has been difficult with fun primarily put on ice

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing put on another sits above it, so the earlier pieces come first
a difficult thing is awkward and contrary, so these letters will not stay in their normal order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Life has been hard, with all the fun put on ice, that is, postponed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Living' looks like a verb or 'life', but here it is the church noun; 'put on ice' sounds like 'suspended' but literally places the earlier letters on top of ICE.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Church of England a living is a paid clerical post such as a parish, which is exactly what a benefice is.

clue.text: Endlessly slow, turning up? Blast!

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning upward means reading from bottom to top
without an end means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: tardy means slow or late

explanation.surface: Someone exasperated that a late person or thing keeps arriving so slowly.
explanation.walkthrough: Trim the last letter to get TARD, then read it upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of annoyance, used as a polite substitute for swearing when something goes wrong.

clue.text: Crime — so it could turn into sexual excitement?

indicators.note: turning into something else means changing form, so these letters are rearranged into a new word

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wry question about whether a crime might become a source of sexual thrill.
explanation.walkthrough: All nine letters of the first three words are reshuffled; the question mark marks the surface as a tease.
explanation.definitionFit: Eroticism is the quality of arousing desire, or the state of being sexually aroused, so it covers sexual excitement.

clue.text: Applaud honoured companion, always

parts.note: CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always

explanation.surface: Clapping for a decorated friend, and doing so forever.
explanation.walkthrough: CH is the post-nominal letters of the Companion of Honour, a British award; e'er is poetic for ever.
explanation.definitionFit: To applaud someone is to show approval by shouting or clapping, which is what crowds do when they cheer.

clue.text: Audacious British party of the wild variety

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
a rave is a wild all-night dance party

explanation.surface: A daring British party that gets out of hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' here is a social event, not a political one, despite 'British' beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Audacious describes someone bold and willing to take risks, which is a close synonym of courageous or daring.

clue.text: Finish in Queer Street, becoming most sore

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so the first piece goes within the second
queer means odd or strange, so the following letters are put in an odd order

parts.note: taken as written
the finish of something is its end

explanation.surface: Ending up in Queer Street, British slang for being in debt, makes a person feel the most hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queer Street' is a fixed phrase meaning financial trouble, so it is hard to split; here 'Queer' rearranges the letters of the next word, and END goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A sore spot is tender to the touch, so the superlative of painful when pressed matches the superlative of sore.

clue.text: Camp bed put down by North American lake

indicators.note: an item put down beside another is placed next to it, so the pieces sit side by side

parts.note: a cot is a small bed, a camp bed in American usage
Lake Erie, one of the Great Lakes

explanation.surface: Someone setting up a folding camp bed beside a lake in North America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Camp bed' reads as one object, but 'Camp' is the definition in its sense of a faction.
explanation.definitionFit: A camp can mean a group of people sharing views or interests, as in rival camps, which is what a clique or coterie is.

clue.text: Member coming to church entrance

parts.note: CH is the abbreviation for church
a limb of the body is a member

explanation.surface: A congregation member arriving at the church door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' wants to be the doorway noun; it is the verb en-TRANCE, to enchant.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance someone is to fill them with delight and wonder, holding their attention, which is the verb sense of charm.

clue.text: Support vehicle returning to get top man

indicators.note: something returning goes back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a cab is a taxi
a king is the man at the top

explanation.surface: A support vehicle coming back to collect the man in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support vehicle' reads as one phrase, but the definition is the first word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Backing is help or endorsement given to a person or cause, a noun synonym for support.

clue.text: Worry female horse audibly in Welsh town

indicators.note: audibly means in a way that can be heard, so the words are judged by sound, not spelling

parts.note: to worry is to care
a filly is a young female horse

explanation.surface: Fretting about a mare somewhere in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: Caerphilly is a town in South Wales known for its castle and a crumbly cheese; said aloud it is 'care filly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Caerphilly is a real town north of Cardiff, so it is a particular example of a place in Wales.

clue.text: Tour leader being listened to and laughed at

indicators.note: what is listened to is heard rather than read, so the sound counts and not the spelling

parts.note: the person who leads a tour

explanation.surface: A tour guide whose patter is heard and then mocked by the group.
explanation.walkthrough: To guy someone is an old-fashioned British verb meaning to ridicule them.
explanation.definitionFit: To guy a person is to mock or make fun of them, so being guyed is being ridiculed or mocked.

clue.text: Bewildered? Worse things happen here, allegedly!

definitions.meaning: second meaning: completes the old consolation 'worse things happen ...'

explanation.walkthrough: The British saying 'worse things happen at sea' consoles someone after a minor misfortune; the clue leaves out its ending.
explanation.definitionFit: Being lost on the ocean is a metaphor for confusion, so the phrase means perplexed or not knowing what to do.

clue.text: Feature of thrillers from American writers in the Florida area?

indicators.note: to be in something is to be enclosed by it, so the earlier pieces sit within the outer one

parts.note: Florida is in the southeast of the United States
US is short for American
pens are things that write

explanation.surface: Wondering whether thrillers by authors from Florida have something in common.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writers' suggests authors, but it is the objects that write; Florida is the southeastern state, giving SE.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrillers rely on tension and anxious uncertainty about what happens next, which is what suspense means.

clue.text: Snoop quietly by railway

parts.note: p is the musical marking piano, meaning quietly
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: Someone spying discreetly beside the railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: P for quiet comes from musical notation, a standard crossword shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: To snoop is to look nosily into other people's affairs, the same verb sense as to be inquisitive or intrusive.

clue.text: Soldiers protecting domestic fortifications

indicators.note: to protect something is to shield it round about, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: paras are paratroopers
a pet is a domestic animal

explanation.surface: Troops guarding the defences of their homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Domestic' suggests home affairs, but here it means a household animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Parapets are low protective walls along the edge of a rampart or roof, part of the defensive works of a castle.

clue.text: Solemn poem with glee somehow unknown?

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters are arranged in some other way

parts.note: taken as written
y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about how a sombre poem could come out full of joy.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the contradiction of a solemn poem containing glee; mathematicians' x, y and z stand for unknowns.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegy is a mournful poem, usually a lament for the dead, so it is a serious, sorrowful kind of verse.

clue.text: Tactile therapist offering service with back-directed 1 down

parts.note: Mass is a church service

indicators.note: pointed backwards means running in the opposite direction, so the letters are read from the end

parts.note: the answer to 1 down is a plant of that kind, and rue is one example

explanation.surface: A hands-on therapist who provides a treatment using an aromatic plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 down is HERB, so the cross-reference stands for any herb; rue is a bitter herb familiar from crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A masseur treats people by rubbing and kneading their muscles, a therapy based on touch.

clue.text: American composer and officer arrive at Heathrow, maybe

parts.note: a cop is a police officer
Heathrow is London's main airport, where planes touch down

explanation.surface: An American musician and a policeman flying into London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks Heathrow as just one example of an airport where a flight might come in.
explanation.definitionFit: Aaron Copland wrote Appalachian Spring and Fanfare for the Common Man, making him a celebrated twentieth-century US composer.

clue.text: Minister and dog had sustenance?

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel dog
taking sustenance means eating, in the past tense

explanation.surface: A clergyman and his dog sharing a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the stilted phrasing for a simple past-tense verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A curate is an assistant clergyman in a parish, so the word names a junior church minister.

clue.text: Brute of a fellow mostly seen round the province

indicators.note: going round something encloses it, so one piece is wrapped around the other
mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
in British usage 'the Province' is Northern Ireland
a male is a man or fellow

explanation.surface: A thuggish man who travels about the region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brute of a fellow' reads as one phrase, but the 'a' belongs to the wordplay; in the UK, Northern Ireland is often called 'the Province'.
explanation.definitionFit: A brute is a beast, and figuratively a coarse, violent person; both senses fit the word for a creature or a savage.

clue.text: Dodgy leader, sanctimonious and English, getting ripped apart

parts.note: pi is informal for piously self-righteous

indicators.note: something pulled apart loses its shape, so these letters are reassembled in a new order

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shady, self-righteous English leader being torn to shreds by critics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ripped apart' sounds like harsh criticism, but it rearranges the letters of 'ripped'. The Pied Piper of Hamelin lured the town's children away.
explanation.definitionFit: The figure from the folk tale led children away with his music, so a person who leads others astray is called this.

clue.text: Chums making hit, going up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going upward means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: to slap is to hit

explanation.surface: Friends who produce a hit record that climbs the charts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit, going up' suggests a chart success; it is a verb for strike, read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Pals and chums are both informal British words for close friends, so they are direct synonyms.

clue.text: What's expected with energy cut?

parts.note: par is the expected standard, as in golf
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A question about what to expect when the power is switched off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Energy cut' reads as a power outage; 'cut' is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To pare is to trim or shave something down, as with fruit skins or budgets, a verb meaning to reduce.

clue.text: identity needed by Man in a manner of speaking

parts.note: ID is short for identity
IOM is the Isle of Man, the island in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: Someone needs proof of identity on the Isle of Man, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital M is the clue: Man is the Isle of Man, a British Crown dependency, abbreviated IOM.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is a fixed expression or a characteristic way of using language, so it describes a style or mode of expression.

clue.text: It was appropriate at one time to assemble

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an archaic adjective for fitting or proper
second meaning: to come together as a group

explanation.surface: Gathering together once seemed the right thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At one time' flags an old-fashioned sense, as in the Prayer Book's 'it is meet and right'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word once meant suitable or fitting, and today as a verb it means to gather or come together.

clue.text: Plant cutter of great power?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old name for the silphium plant and related umbellifers
second meaning: a focused beam that can slice through metal

explanation.surface: A heavy-duty tool for chopping down vegetation.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant sense is obscure, so the second definition does the work; the question mark admits the cutter is a beam of light, not a blade.
explanation.definitionFit: A laser beam concentrates intense light energy to slice materials, and laser is also a dictionary name for an aromatic umbelliferous herb.

clue.text: Thrill produced by bird, one by lake after dusk?

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
Roman numeral one
L is the abbreviation for lake
after dusk the hour is late

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher's excitement at a bird beside a lake in the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that 'after dusk' is only one example of lateness.
explanation.definitionFit: To titillate is to excite or stimulate pleasurably, which is a verb synonym of to give a person a thrill.
